meters.label: Requests hit by bugs before noticed
Days until real users reach the new system

frames.narration: A legacy shop has 8 slices and serves 369 thousand requests a day. The new versions will have 9 hidden bugs, some loud and some firing once per 1,000 requests, and nobody knows which yet.

Big-bang plan: build everything, switch once. No real user touches the new system for 169 days. Then 100 percent of traffic switches at once, with no shadow run: the 9 bugs hit 22,269 requests, because with the legacy system retired the fix has to go forward and takes 5 days.

Strangler plan: put a router in front, still sending everything to legacy. Then build one slice at a time. The first users reach the new system on day 22, and the most traffic switched in any one step is 16 percent of all traffic.

Parity checks: each slice first runs in shadow mode, answered by legacy and compared against the new one, with 500 replayed requests per slice. That catches 7 of the 9 bugs before any user sees them. The 2 rare ones slip through, and cost 49 requests across the ramp.

The plausible shortcut: ramp traffic but skip the parity checks. 0 of 9 bugs are caught early, so users find them: 670 requests are hit. One bug is too quiet to ever trigger the alert and stays silent after the migration is done.

Ramp too big makes it worse. Moving each slice at once without parity checks costs 4,461 requests, against 69 with parity checks at the same 500 shadow requests. The step size and the shadow run work together.

The over-applied version: slices of one endpoint, 24 slices. First users arrive on day 8, the widest step is 5 percent of traffic and bugs cost only 36 requests. But 24 slices have to be routed and tracked, and 12 data links cross the old and new boundary at the worst moment, against 4 with 8 slices.

So slice along real seams, prove parity in shadow mode with enough requests to see rare bugs, ramp in steps with a rollback that stays alive, count the data links you will have to keep consistent, and give the migration an end date.
